A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ULTra and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 has no appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–G. Retained material can be matched reliably across the substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation results on COCO-Stuff, PASCAL VOC, and Potsdam, object-selection measurements, layer-depth analyses, and qualitative LLM interpretation examples.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of method variants, additional backbones, Cityscapes, perturbations, and parameter sensitivity.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's norm/energy-based interpretation, v2 introduces the summed-coordinate ULTraS variant and learned ULTraW projections. Sections 3.2 and 4.1 add token-specific, normalized projection vectors trained through a self-consistency loss under input perturbations while keeping the backbone unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cityscapes urban-street segmentation and masked/noisy image scenarios for interpretability evaluation. COCO-Stuff 27, PASCAL VOC, Potsdam-3, and the existing language-data coverage remain. These additions extend the established visual interpretation and segmentation scope.

E2.justification: The COCO-Stuff comparison adds STEGO+HP and TransFGU; TransFGU was already compared on PASCAL VOC in v1. STEGO+HP also participates in the new Cityscapes comparison. The existing PASCAL VOC and Potsdam comparator families are retained.

E3.justification: v2 reports main segmentation experiments with a predefined cluster count, while retaining v1's threshold-based setting in Appendix F. It expands beyond CLIP ViT-B/32 to additional CLIP and DINO backbones, introduces 256-sample projection training, and adds equal-area perturbation tests measuring embedding distance for ten randomly selected tokens per image. The LLM alignment settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 retains the original depth analysis and adds a ViT-L/14 depth study, positive/negative masking and noise tests, ITIoU sensitivity to threshold and depth, and clustering-threshold sweeps. Appendix B and Figure 8 also add challenging segmentation cases examining annotation mismatches.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new random-token sampling specifies an evaluation design, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for variants, backbones, Cityscapes, perturbations, and sensitivity analyses. Examples include 38.2 COCO-Stuff mIoU for CLIP ViT-L/14 ULTraW and 26.5 Cityscapes mIoU for DINO ViT-B/16 ULTraW. These are new configurations, not same-setting gains over v1. v1's segmentation scores are preserved exactly in Table 8, and its ITIoU scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds scalar-function definitions, weighted-gradient derivations, a unit-norm constrained projection-learning problem, and the self-consistency objective in Sections 3.2 and 4.1. These substantially extend the mathematical formulation. The original Transformer equations move to Appendix G; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from training-free interpretation and segmentation to a framework incorporating learned external refinement. Perturbation-based validation becomes a headline contribution, and the introduction adds an explicit first-to-directly-investigate-latent-token-interpretability claim. The original segmentation and cross-modal applicability claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning annotation mismatches, clustering failure with small patches, and expensive per-token gradient computation. Appendix A introduces a semantic-abstraction versus spatial-precision explanation for deeper-layer degradation. The perturbation experiments also support a new interpretation of explanation-map reliability.

D1.justification: v2 adds backbone dimensions, the 256-example projection-training budget, and zero-masking/Gaussian-noise specifications, including noise strength 0.3. Reported hardware changes from eight RTX 4090 24GB GPUs to four A100 80GB GPUs. These disclosures remain incomplete: fixed cluster counts and the projection optimizer and training schedule are unspecified.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around Transformer interpretation, weakly supervised segmentation, and latent embeddings. New coverage includes LeGrad, token reduction, register tokens, and GroupViT. Much of v1's general interpretability and chain-of-thought/theory-of-mind discussion disappears, and its detailed criticism of INVITE is shortened.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related work, methodology narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. v2 separates application formulations from experimental results and reorganizes retained architecture descriptions, dataset information, and analyses into Appendices A–G. Terminology shifts from relevance maps toward explanation maps.

P2.justification: v2 adds an architecture diagram, perturbation and challenging-case illustrations, and several analysis plots. Tables gain backbone columns, variant groupings, and comparison arrows. All six original figures are retained or reformatted, including v1 Figure 1 becoming v2 Figure 13 and the original depth plots becoming Figure 7. The appendices introduce substantial single-column layout changes.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly validates explanations through segmentation overlap and qualitative examples. v2's controlled positive/negative perturbation tests directly examine whether highlighted regions influence latent representations, substantially strengthening the empirical foundation. Broader backbone evaluation, sensitivity analyses, and explicit computational and clustering limitations further improve assessment of applicability. The learned variant remains incompletely specified and does not improve every reported setting, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.
